etymology_text:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-
Proto-Indo-European *-s
Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s
Proto-Indo-European *dʰh₁sós
Proto-Hellenic *tʰehós
Ancient Greek θεός
From Proto-Hellenic *tʰehós (whence also Mycenaean Greek 𐀳𐀃 (te-o)), a thematicization of amphikinetic Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁-s-(s) ~ *dʰh₁-s-és, from *dʰeh₁- (“to do, to put, to place”) + *-s (s-stem forming suffix). Exact cognate with Phrygian devos, which could be closely related under the Graeco-Phrygian hypothesis.
Related to Old Armenian դիք (dikʻ, “gods”) and Latin fēria (“festival day”), fānum (“temple”) and fēstus (“festive”).
Despite its similarity in form and meaning, the word is not related to Latin deus; the two come from different roots. A true cognate of deus is Ζεύς (Zeús).

etymology_text:
From Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- (“to cut off, separate, free”) (which Beekes reconstructs as *lh₁u-). Cognates include Latin luō (“expiate, pay”), Sanskrit लुनाति (lunā́ti, “to sever, cut forth, destroy, annihilate”), English loose, and possibly Old Armenian լուծանեմ (lucanem) and Albanian lirë.
According to Beekes, the stem vowel was originally short (λῠ-), lengthened only later in Attic and sometimes in Homer (λῡ-) due to the influence of a laryngeal. The upsilon remains short (ῠ) before temporal endings beginning with ⟨κ, θ, μ⟩ and all derivatives, but the prosody of compounds remains that of λῡ́ω (lū́ō).
Derivatives, from the stems λῠσ- (lŭs-), λῠσῐ- (lŭsĭ-) (compounds with λῡσῐ- (lūsĭ-)), λῠτ- (lŭt-).
Unrelated to κωλῡ́ω (kōlū́ō, “prevent”), ὄλλῡμῐ (óllūmĭ, “destroy, lose”) or λύσσᾰ (lússă, “rage”).

etymology_text: From Proto-Hellenic *ptólis, from Proto-Indo-European *tpólHis, from *tpelH- (“fortification; city”). The early form πτόλις (ptólis) shows metathesis tp > pt because Ancient Greek stop clusters always end in a coronal. Cognate with Sanskrit पुर॑ (púra, “fortress, city, dwelling”) and Lithuanian pilis (“stronghold”). Irregular accent on genitive πόλεως (póleōs) is due to a quantitative metathesis from older πόληος (pólēos); genitive plural imitates genitive singular.

etymology_text:
PIE word
 *h₁én
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”), cognate with Latin in, Old Armenian ի (i), Albanian një, English in.
The dative is from the Proto-Indo-European locative; the genitive is an innovated Greek associative; the accusative is from the pre-Proto-Indo-European directional.

en hōî dè hoûtoi tòn prokeímenon pónon ergázonto, en toútōi ho pezòs hápas sullelegménos háma Xérxēi eporeúeto es Sárdis,[…]
examples.english:
Translation by George Rawlinson
During the time that all these labours were in progress, the land army which had been collected was marching with Xerxes towards Sardis, […]

κἀν ᾧ τὸ κεῖσε δεῦρό τ’ ἐξορμώμεθα,
ὁρῶμεν αὐτὴν ἀμφιπλῆγι φασγάνῳ
πλευρὰν ὑφ’ ἧπαρ καὶ φρένας πεπληγμένην.
kan hōî tò keîse deûró t’ exormṓmetha,
horômen autḕn amphiplêgi phasgánōi

raw_glosses: (time) in; at; or during the time of
[with ᾧ (hōî)]
glosses: in; at; or during the time of

args.notes: The clipped dative plural forms τοῖς (toîs) and τῇς (tēîs) occasionally occur.

etymology_text: From Proto-Hellenic *hó *hā́ *tó, from Proto-Indo-European *só *séh₂ *tód. There are many cognates, including Sanskrit स (sá), सा (sā́) तद् (tád), Old Church Slavonic тъ (tŭ), та (ta), то (to), and Old English sē, sēo, þæt (English the, that).
